item.title: Teleportation of Logical Qubits using Lattice Surgery with Superconducting Circuits
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Demonstrated fault-tolerant lattice-surgery teleportation between two distance-three surface-code logical qubits on a 41-transmon chip. Circuit depletion improved logical success probabilities from 0.57 to 0.65 for Z basis states and from 0.66 to 0.73 for X basis states.

Grade 0.398 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Luca Hofele, Yongxin Song, Áron Márton, Ian Hesner, Ilya Besedin, Jakob Ekert, Jonathan Trebst, Franccois Swiadek, Felix Henrich, Dante Colao Zanúz, Mohsen Bahrami Panah, Lukas Bödeker, Nicholas Gialouris, Chrysander D. Hagen, Marek Pechal, Jean Claude Besse, Markus Müller, Christoph Hellings, Andreas Wallraff

Figure

Error-corrected logical expectation values across three teleportation circuits (fully modular, partially depleted, and fully depleted) for four logical eigenstates. Depleting non-essential stabilizer rounds increases teleported output fidelity.

Asks

How do logical observables evolve throughout fault-tolerant lattice surgery, and can circuit depletion optimize logical teleportation performance?

Before

Fully modular logical teleportation circuit achieved logical expectation values of |obreak⟨mSmZZˆL2⟩|=0.14 and |⟨mXXˆL2⟩|=0.32.

But

Demonstrated for Pauli eigenstates only; full quantum state tomography not implemented. Physical error rates remain above fault-tolerance threshold.

Tools

41 frequency-tunable transmon superconducting circuit · distance-three rotated planar surface code · flux-activated CZ gates · multiplexed dispersive readout with Purcell filters · lattice surgery

Abstract

Demonstrating a quantum advantage when solving large-scale computational problems on a quantum computer requires the correction of errors that occur due to limitations in control accuracy and coherence. Using the concept of quantum error correction, fault-tolerant logical qubits can be realized and manipulated with logical single- and two-qubit gates. In this paper, we experimentally analyze fault-tolerant lattice-surgery, which is a key primitive that enables operations between logical qubits realized in the surface-code. Using this primitive, we demonstrate the teleportation of logical states between two distance-three logical qubits realized in a superconducting circuit composed of 41 physical qubits. Throughout this process, we study the step-by-step transfer of logical information from a source to a target logical qubit by characterizing the time evolution of logical observables. We find that repeated execution of stabilizer measurements, after merging two surface-code patches, restores fault tolerance and yields increased fidelity of the teleported state. When optimizing the protocol in terms of gate count and sequence duration, we observe further improvements in fidelity. Our work offers new insights into the optimization of fault-tolerant lattice-surgery operations, while also providing a comprehensive description of the physical device and gate sequences used. We expect the efficient implementation of increasingly complex logical circuits to enhance the performance of future fault-tolerant quantum computers.

item.title: Predicting Quantum Mpemba Effects from Quantum Speed Limits
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Short-time Quantum Speed Limits (QSLs) predict Quantum Mpemba Effect orderings at times t∗≪τ prior to trajectory crossings, yielding recall P≈0.8 and precision enrichment PE≈3 in collective spins and open spin chains.

Grade 0.379 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “thermalization, many-body localization and quantum scars in driven systems” · Andrea Nava, Rosario Fazio, Reinhold Egger

Figure

Recall P, precision enrichment PE, and false discovery rate vs observation time t∗ for a collective-spin model (S=10). Short-time indicators reliably predict Mpemba inversions when early trajectory crossings dominate (a), but require times past the inverse Liouvillian gap when late crossings dominate (b).

Asks

Can features of initial transient dynamics and Quantum Speed Limits anticipate anomalous Quantum Mpemba Effects before a system nears stationarity?

But

Predictions degrade when late-time trajectory crossings dominate. Analytical short-time expansion sTD=−K assumes non-singular initial velocity V=ℒρ0, requiring full finite-time indicators for pure-state ensembles.

Tools

Trace-distance and relative-purity quantum speed limits · Short-time geometric scores (s_TD = -K, s_RP = B) · Lindblad master equation · Exact diagonalization

Abstract

Can anomalous Quantum Mpemba Effects be anticipated before a system comes close to its stationary state? We employ Quantum Speed Limits as geometric indicators of Quantum Mpemba Effects, arguing that Mpemba physics is already imprinted in speed limits by benchmarking dissipative qubits and open spin chains. Our results show that short-time speed limits can predict Quantum Mpemba Effects at low cost and with reasonable precision over broad parameter regimes. This predictive power implies a useful application of speed limits for open many-body quantum systems.

item.title: Local interference algorithms for observables in large random circuits
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Observable interference corrections decay as exp⁡(−constd) in space-time volume d. Simulating time-ordered and out-of-time-ordered correlators in random circuits achieves polynomial run-time scaling in circuit size and target precision.

Grade 0.361 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “analog quantum simulation of lattice models on cold atoms or superconducting ar…” · Philippe Suchsland, Brayden Ware, Vladislav D. Kurilovich, Vadim Smelyanskiy, Kostyantyn Kechedzhi

Figure

Squared relative error ϵr2 plotted against spatial partition width ℓ at T=500 and extrapolated T→∞. Error decays super-exponentially with partition width as the number of combined partitions R increases from 1 to 6.

Asks

Can classical trajectory-sampling algorithms simulate quantum physical observables in typical random circuits with controlled error and polynomial efficiency despite interference effects?

But

Demonstrated for 1d brickwork random Haar circuits and 1d U(1)-conserving random circuits; ensemble-averaged analyses and small-to-moderate circuit depths.

Tools

Monte Carlo trajectory sampling · tensor network contraction · replica statistical mechanics models · inclusion-exclusion partition subtractions · matrix product state master equation evolution

Abstract

In quantum dynamics, it is generally believed that interference effects lead to a sign problem for classical Monte Carlo sampling methods, rendering sampling ineffective. In this paper we show that this is generically not the case for the task of simulating the evolution of observables in random instances of circuit dynamics. Specifically, we consider two examples of observables which give large signals despite the randomness of the dynamics: first order out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) in unstructured random circuits without conservation laws and time-ordered charge-charge correlators (TOCs) in particle number-preserving random circuits. We show that these observables can be approximated by classical stochastic processes and that these approximations can be systematically improved with a series expansion that incorporates coherent corrections associated with clusters of gates. We design and implement algorithms that combine Monte Carlo sampling and tensor network methods to approximate the series. We observe numerically that the computational complexity of approximating TOCs and OTOCs scales polynomially in the circuit size and in the target precision. We study the accuracy of these algorithms by directly mapping their ensemble-averaged errors to partition functions of replica statistical models, allowing for perturbative analysis and numerics in 1d brickwork geometries. Our theoretical analysis explains the empirical observation of polynomial complexity of these algorithms and is consistent with polynomial complexity extending to arbitrarily small precision and to the thermodynamic limit.

item.title: Simplifying models of noisy stabilizer QEC on leakage qubits by Pauli twirling
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Noisy stabilizer QEC cycles with leakage reduce under leakage-dephased Pauli twirling to a classical Markov chain over joint syndrome and leakage patterns, with logical Pauli channels attached to each joint transition.

Grade 0.353 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Alex Kwiatkowski, Aaron J. Friedman

Asks

How to model multi-cycle logical performance of noisy stabilizer QEC when physical qubits suffer leakage errors?

Before

Prior framework modeled stabilizer cycles under Pauli-stochastic noise as Markov processes over syndrome states, but did not handle leakage states.

But

Applies after twirling; assumes stabilizer codes and leakage states governed by conditional computational Pauli channels.

Tools

leakage-dephased Pauli twirling · transfer-matrix formalism · Markov chain over joint syndrome-leakage patterns

Abstract

The growing capabilities of quantum error-correction (QEC) experiments make it increasingly important to develop methods that predict or assess logical performance over many QEC cycles. Prior work has shown that a stabilizer QEC cycle subject to Pauli-stochastic noise can be modeled by a classical Markov process over syndrome states, with a logical Pauli channel attached to each syndrome transition. Here, we extend this framework to systems in which physical qubits are subject to leakage. We first develop the theory of leakage-dephased Pauli twirling and show that twirled processes can be expressed in terms of Pauli maps on the computational subspace, conditioned on transitions between leakage patterns. We apply this theory to noisy stabilizer QEC with leakage, demonstrating that a QEC cycle with leakage can be modeled by a classical Markov process over the joint syndrome and leakage patterns, with a logical Pauli channel attached to each joint transition. Finally, we derive a transfer-matrix description of repeated QEC cycles and an exact transfer-matrix expression for the success probability of a QEC memory experiment. This framework connects leaky error models of the individual components of the QEC cycle to many-cycle logical performance and provides a foundation for logical characterization and benchmarking methods that can account for leakage.

item.title: Circuit compilation in the quspect quantum SDK: selecting routings after coupling-constrained resynthesis
item.description:
Worth a look new method — quspect compiler uses 0.616 times as many two-qubit gates as Qiskit O3 (95% bootstrap interval 0.555–0.679) at 0.592 times the depth across 55 arXiv circuits on five topologies.

Grade 0.346 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Xusheng Xu, Runqing Zhang, Hongtao Xue, Jize Han, Jingwei Wen, Ruoyu Zhou, Lei Jin, Xiaoxiao Hu, Gui-Lu Long

Figure

Geometric-mean ratios of two-qubit gate count and circuit depth relative to Qiskit O3 for 275 cases (55 circuits across five coupling topologies). Values below 1.0 indicate smaller gate counts or shallower depth than Qiskit O3.

Asks

How can circuit compilation combine layout routing and synthesis to prevent routed SWAP gates from inflating post-synthesis gate count and depth?

Before

BQSKit level 2 reached 0.853 and tket 0.930 relative to Qiskit O3 two-qubit gate counts.

But

arXiv set aggregate results informed development; loses to Qiskit on random Clifford circuits on 127- and 156-qubit devices; outputs verified numerically to 10−9 tolerance per matrix element.

Tools

coupling-constrained resynthesis · parity-state A* search · merge-aware routing large-neighborhood search · numerical three-qubit block instantiation

Code. https://github.com/QuSpect/quspect

Abstract

quspect is an open-source quantum computing SDK that provides circuit construction, C++ state-vector simulation with adjoint gradients, support for variational and combinatorial-optimization algorithms, Hamiltonian simulation, control-pulse envelopes and backends for several cloud quantum processors. Here we describe and evaluate its circuit compiler. Routing and synthesis interact: inserting a SWAP can change the circuit structure that later optimization exploits. At its highest optimization level, the compiler evaluates a screened set of routing candidates by their cost after coupling-constrained resynthesis. The pipeline combines parity-state A* search for small CNOT-phase regions, heuristic synthesis for larger regions, and numerical three-qubit instantiation with a per-block 10^-9 check. For a fixed phase polynomial, A* certifies the minimum CX count when it reaches a goal within budget. On an evaluation set of 55 circuits from 41 arXiv papers on five topologies, the compiler uses 0.616 times as many two-qubit gates as Qiskit O3 (95% circuit-cluster bootstrap interval 0.555-0.679) at 0.592 times its depth. BQSKit level 2 reaches 0.853 and tket 0.930. On a 17-qubit superconducting processor, the compiled circuits had the fewest CZ gates in all six scenarios of the main run. Ablations assess the contributions within the integrated pipeline.

item.title: Nonlinearity-preserving quantum simulation of flows in the early fault-tolerant regime
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Simulating cylinder wake dynamics to 1% relative root-mean-square field error requires estimated 1.62 h on about 560,000 physical qubits in a surface code.

Grade 0.344 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Hansol Noh (David), Unam Oh (David), Sangkyu Baek (David), Doyeol (David), Ahn

Asks

Can early fault-tolerant quantum algorithms achieve end-to-end feasibility for propagating nonlinear fluid ensembles under grid-dependent circuit costs?

But

Polynomial reduced-order model, cylinder wake flow approaching saturation, resource estimates based on rotated surface codes, hardware run limited to radial coordinate with reference-circuit error mitigation.

Tools

sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy) · Walsh-synthesized Koopman-von Neumann (KvN) transport · surface-code resource estimation · IBM quantum hardware

Abstract

Ensemble prediction of nonlinear dynamics propagates a probability density whose linear transport equation retains the nonlinear drift, but grid-dependent circuit costs leave end-to-end feasibility in early fault-tolerant quantum computing unresolved. We couple polynomial reduced-order models fitted by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics to Walsh-synthesized Koopman-von Neumann (KvN) transport and surface-code resource estimation. At fixed model dimension and drift degree, per-step transport rotation counts scale polylogarithmically with cells per reduced coordinate. Balancing model accuracy against circuit costs makes reduced-model polynomial degree a design variable for early fault-tolerant quantum simulation. For a cylinder wake approaching saturation, preparation, propagation and sampling to 1% relative root-mean-square field error against the radial model are estimated to take 1.62 h on about 560,000 physical qubits. Estimated three-coordinate wake runtimes span hours to weeks below one million qubits. IBM hardware experiments demonstrate nonlinear radial KvN transport for this wake, using reference circuits to mitigate noise.

item.title: Logical error prediction and geometry selection for rectangular surface codes under biased circuit-level noise
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Response coefficients derived strictly from an unbiased reference circuit predict finite-bias circuit-level logical error rates with a median fold error of 1.09, cutting physical qubit counts by up to 42.4% (standard depolarizing) and 26.2% (superconducting-inspired) relative to square codes at physical error rate p=0.004 and target logical error rate PL,target=10−3.

Grade 0.340 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Youshin Chung, Yujin Kang, Jun Heo

Figure

Physical qubit count as a function of idle noise bias for validated rectangular surface codes versus unrotated square code baselines at p=0.004 and PL,target=10−3.

Asks

Can the logical error response to a localized circuit-level bias be inferred from an unbiased reference circuit and transferred to finite-bias conditions without geometry- or bias-specific response fitting?

Before

Neglecting bias response gives a median fold error of 1.28, while mapping the full idle-channel change directly into the baseline parameter yields 3.18.

But

Unrotated rectangular surface codes only; evaluated at bias ratios η∈{1,2,3}, 0.003≤p≤0.008, and for memory experiments run over r=max⁡(L1,L2) rounds.

Tools

Stim and PyMatching · Score-function logical sensitivity estimation · Ordinary least-squares regression · Sinter Monte Carlo sampling

Abstract

Realistic quantum hardware often exhibits biased noise, but at the circuit level this bias may affect only a subset of operations and need not be transferred uniformly to logical errors. The logical response to a given physical bias is therefore central to selecting resource-efficient surface code geometries. Here, we study unrotated rectangular surface codes under standard depolarizing and superconducting-inspired circuit-level noise models. We first construct geometry-dependent logical error rate models from unbiased circuit-level simulations. We then use logical sensitivities to compare the responses to localized idle-bias and global physical error perturbations, defining logical-error-type-dependent response coefficients from an unbiased reference circuit without fitting to finite-bias data. These coefficients are incorporated through effective error parameters, yielding a median fold error of 1.09 over the evaluated finite-bias conditions. item.arxave:abstract: Realistic quantum hardware often exhibits biased noise, but at the circuit level this bias may affect only a subset of operations and need not be transferred uniformly to logical errors. The logical response to a given physical bias is therefore central to selecting resource-efficient surface code geometries. Here, we study unrotated rectangular surface codes under standard depolarizing and superconducting-inspired circuit-level noise models. We first construct geometry-dependent logical error rate models from unbiased circuit-level simulations. We then use logical sensitivities to compare the responses to localized idle-bias and global physical error perturbations, defining logical-error-type-dependent response coefficients from an unbiased reference circuit without fitting to finite-bias data. These coefficients are incorporated through effective error parameters, yielding a median fold error of 1.09 over the evaluated finite-bias conditions. Geometries selected by the model are validated through direct biased circuit-level simulations. At a physical error rate of 0.004 and a target logical error rate of 10^{-3}, the validated rectangular codes reduce physical qubit overhead by up to 42.4% and 26.2% under the two noise models, respectively, relative to unrotated square codes. These results provide a practical link between circuit-level bias response and resource-efficient surface code design.
